content_voiceover: This reference table lists the syndromes associated with Wilms tumor risk, and the four boxed at the top are the ones most likely to be tested. WAGR syndrome, from an eleven p one three deletion of WT1, presents with aniridia, genitourinary anomalies, and delayed-onset renal failure, and carries about a thirty percent Wilms tumor risk. Denys-Drash syndrome, from a point mutation in the zinc-finger region of WT1, also at eleven p one three, presents with ambiguous genitalia and diffuse mesangial sclerosis, and carries a very high risk, over ninety percent. Frasier syndrome, from a point mutation in the WT1 intron nine donor splice site, presents with ambiguous genitalia, streak gonads, and focal segmental glomerulosclerosis, with a lower risk around eight percent. And Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome, from dysregulation of imprinted genes including IGF2 and H19 at eleven p fifteen, presents with organomegaly, large birth weight, macroglossia, omphalocele, hemihypertrophy, ear pits and creases, and neonatal hypoglycemia, with about a five percent Wilms tumor risk. Further down the table are rarer associations, Simpson-Golabi-Behmel syndrome, Li-Fraumeni syndrome, mosaic variegated aneuploidy, Fanconi anemia D1, and several others, each with its own locus and estimated risk.
keypoints: WAGR, eleven p one three deletion of WT1, about thirty percent Wilms tumor risk
Denys-Drash, WT1 zinc-finger mutation, ambiguous genitalia, over ninety percent risk
Frasier syndrome, WT1 splice-site mutation, streak gonads, about eight percent risk
Beckwith-Wiedemann, eleven p fifteen, IGF2 and H19 dysregulation, about five percent risk
keypoint_voiceover: Four syndromes to distinguish by their WT1 or eleven p fifteen lesion. WAGR and Denys-Drash both hit WT1 at eleven p thirteen, but Denys-Drash carries a much higher Wilms tumor risk, over ninety percent, because it is a specific zinc-finger mutation rather than a deletion. Frasier syndrome is the milder cousin with a splice-site mutation and lower risk. And Beckwith-Wiedemann is the odd one out, driven by imprinted gene dysregulation at eleven p fifteen rather than WT1 itself, presenting with overgrowth features instead of genitourinary anomalies.
